oludeniz-babadag.best_time: Tandems fly all day from morning to sunset; thermals are strongest from 11:00 until 15:00–16:00; evening flights are calmer
oludeniz-babadag.access: The Babadağ Teleferik cable car from the foot of the mountain near Ölüdeniz to the 1,200, 1,700 and 1,800 m stations; there's also a road up the mountain — operators drive clients up by minibus (about 45–60 minutes)
oludeniz-babadag.xc_note: The site is first and foremost for tandems, acro and SIV over the lagoon; XC flights inland into the Lycian mountains are possible, but that's not its main specialty
oludeniz-babadag.rules: Independent pilots need a licence (IPPI card) and insurance; flight registration and takeoff tickets go through the Babadağ Teleferik operator (fee for the ride up and takeoff); after landing, you must close your flight in the app. Tandems have priority on takeoff
oludeniz-babadag.landing: Landing on the promenade/beach at Belcekız in Ölüdeniz: big but crowded, with the approach over water and the beach; backup — Butterfly Valley
oludeniz-babadag.events: The Ölüdeniz Air Games international festival (every October; the 25th edition in 2025): acro shows, competitions; Acro Battle Ölüdeniz. In 2023 more than 224,000 flights were made from Babadağ in one season
pros: A huge height difference with views of the Blue Lagoon
Cable car to the takeoffs
Long season, flyable days almost year-round
Lots of operators, some Russian-speaking
SIV and acro over water
cons: Very crowded on takeoff and in the air
Tandems have priority, so solo pilots wait
Landing on a cramped beach
High prices with middlemen
oludeniz-babadag.tandem_price_note: Usually 6,000–7,500 TL (≈$150–200) with local operators; 20–45-minute flight; photos/video ~$30–50 extra. Russian-speaking middlemen charge €189–200 with transfer
school_notes: APPI school: beginner courses, SIV, tandems, gear rental, XC guiding
APPI school: SIV and acro courses over the sea, tandems
Tandem with Russian-speaking support and transfer, ~€189 per person (the offer was temporarily suspended at the time of checking)

pamukkale-dinamit-tepe.description: Pamukkale is Turkey's second most popular tandem spot: a flight from Dinamit Tepe hill over the white travertines and ancient Hierapolis. Local schools also have their training slope here, and the Çökelez mountain takeoff (1,670 m) delivers some of the best XC flights in the country — the Turkish record is 255 km. A coastal alternative is Alanya: tandems from takeoffs at 600–700 m with a landing on Cleopatra Beach, and lots of Russian-speaking agencies (from ~€99).
pamukkale-dinamit-tepe.rating_basis: Tandems over a UNESCO site (Turkey's second most popular after Babadağ), a training slope for schools, serious XC from Çökelez (the 255 km Turkish record, a PWC round)
pamukkale-dinamit-tepe.hazards: Strong summer thermals, dust (June–August), easterly wind on Dinamit; don't land on the travertines — it's a protected area
pamukkale-dinamit-tepe.crowd_note: Lots of tandems at once in the morning and at sunset, but the takeoff is wide
pamukkale-dinamit-tepe.season: Flyable year-round (around 20,000 tandems a year); best months May–September, for record XC July–August (strong air); May and September are the most comfortable
pamukkale-dinamit-tepe.transfer: Denizli Çardak airport ~1 h; ~20 minutes from Denizli; ~3.5–4 h from Antalya, ~3.5 h from Ölüdeniz
pamukkale-dinamit-tepe.takeoffs: Dinamit Tepe 720 m (a wide west-facing takeoff, ~2.5 km from the village); the Çökelez mountain takeoff 1,670 m (S, also works in westerly wind, landing at ~1,000 m) — for XC flights; in May pilots sometimes launch straight off the travertines and soar along the 160-metre cliffs
pamukkale-dinamit-tepe.wind_note: Best in W–NW wind of up to 25–30 km/h; usually steady, with occasional gusts. Easterly wind on Dinamit is a warning sign. Towards evening, in westerly wind, pilots soar over the travertines for hours
pamukkale-dinamit-tepe.best_time: Tandems in the morning and at sunset (views of the travertines and Hierapolis); in summer, thermals from midday, and the wind usually picks up after 16:00
pamukkale-dinamit-tepe.access: Dirt roads lead to both takeoffs (4×4 preferable); tandem operators pick you up from hotels in Pamukkale, ~15 minutes up
pamukkale-dinamit-tepe.xc_note: From the Çökelez mountain takeoff, flights of 100+ km to the N and NE are routine, with cloud base up to 3,000–3,800 m; the site and Turkish record is 255 km (Hakan Akçalar). A Paragliding World Cup round was held here in 2011
pamukkale-dinamit-tepe.rules: Pilots must register on the Cappadocia University centre's website (shmpamukkaleparasut.kapadokya.edu.tr); the fee for launching from the “green carpet” is 250 TL (2024); IPPI card and insurance
pamukkale-dinamit-tepe.landing: Big open fields by the village of Pamukkale (~366 m); at Çökelez, landing at ~1,000 m
pamukkale-dinamit-tepe.events: Paragliding World Cup round (2011); the 255 km Turkish record was launched from Çökelez
pros: Views of the travertines and Hierapolis
Flyable almost year-round
Training slope and schools
Strong XC from Çökelez in summer
cons: Heat and dust in summer
Strict rules in the protected UNESCO area
Little information in Russian
pamukkale-dinamit-tepe.tandem_price_note: 15–30-minute tandem over the travertines and Hierapolis; agency prices vary considerably
school_notes: Contact for guiding and courses listed by Cross Country Magazine
Local air sports club

chelan-butte.description: Chelan Butte is a mountain in the Cascade foothills between Lake Chelan and the Columbia River, and a classic US summer XC site. From the south-facing takeoff, powerful, wide thermals lift you to 3,000 m, and the wind carries pilots north-east over a vast plateau full of fields to land in.
chelan-butte.rating_basis: Cross Country: one of the best summer XC sites in the US — powerful thermals, high cloud base, a flat plateau and almost no airspace restrictions
chelan-butte.hazards: Dust devils on takeoff; strong thermals (up to 10 m/s); launching from “Between The Rocks” there are rocks on both sides — hold your heading until you're clear; low-flying military aircraft; hot, remote landing fields
chelan-butte.crowd_note: Crowded only during summer competitions and fly-ins
chelan-butte.region: Chelan, Washington State — between Lake Chelan and the Columbia River
chelan-butte.season: Flyable year-round, but the road to takeoff is usually open from mid-April until the first snow; the best XC conditions are in June–August (flyable March to October according to Cross Country)
chelan-butte.transfer: ~45 minutes from Wenatchee; a little over 3 hours by car from Seattle; on XC flights you need a retrieve driver or hitchhiking
chelan-butte.takeoffs: The launch area on the summit (~1,130 m, by the radio towers): Ants — facing SE, Between the Rocks — facing S (between rock outcrops), Green Monster — facing SW, Lakeside — facing NW (best in light wind and for less experienced pilots)
chelan-butte.wind_note: The south-facing takeoffs start working around 11:00; the surface flow usually carries you north-east over the plateau towards Mansfield. Thermals are big and wide, climbs up to ~10 m/s, up to ~3,000 m above the terrain; cloud base 2,700–3,300 m above the mountain, higher over the flats. In light wind, use the NW-facing Lakeside takeoff
chelan-butte.best_time: Launches from ~11:00; in the afternoon, strong thermals and dust devils on takeoff — pick your cycle carefully
chelan-butte.access: From US-97A in the Lakeside area (Chelan), up Chelan Butte Road: the lower part is paved, the upper part dirt/gravel, so you need high clearance or 4×4; the road is usually open from mid-April until the first snow — don't drive it in wet weather. You can also hike up — the trail starts opposite the Junkyard landing field. Parking requires a Washington Discover Pass
chelan-butte.xc_note: In summer, long downwind flights over the flat plateau are typical, as are out-and-returns and triangles; experts fly more than 200 km; no airspace restrictions almost all the way to Spokane (~160 km)
chelan-butte.rules: Current USHPA membership is mandatory (temporary membership is available for foreigners), plus a P3/H3 rating or equivalent; P2/H2 pilots only under instructor supervision; all pilots join the Lake Chelan Flyers club. Carry a shovel and a 10/BC fire extinguisher in your car on the mountain, no smoking or fires on takeoff; motors and parakites are banned. The airspace is open almost all the way to Spokane; military aircraft fly low
chelan-butte.landing: The main landing field is Chelan Falls Park (soccer field, ~215 m) by the Columbia River: land only in the designated area south of the field and check the park schedule; backup — Junkyard (~365 m). The Lone Pine and Chelan airport landing fields are closed. Along XC routes, lots of fields and public land
chelan-butte.events: Annual fly-ins and competitions on Chelan Butte (dates on the Lake Chelan Flyers club website)
pros: Powerful thermals and high cloud base
Flights of 100–200+ km over a flat plateau
Almost no airspace restrictions
Beautiful views of the Cascades and volcanoes
cons: Strong, rough summer thermals — not for beginners
XC retrieves needed
Little information on tandems
chelan-butte.airport: EAT — Wenatchee, ~30–40 min; SEA — Seattle, ~3+ h
school_notes: The club is the USHPA chapter that runs the site: takeoff and landing guide, rules, membership

owens-valley-gunter.description: The Owens Valley between the Sierra Nevada and the White Mountains is one of the most powerful and famous XC arenas in the world: cloud base up to 6,000 m, desert thermals and flights of hundreds of kilometres. It's not a place for tourist tandems, but for experienced pilots in spring and autumn.
owens-valley-gunter.rating_basis: Cross Country: a legendary valley of big XC flights and records, cloud base up to 6,000 m; but very harsh conditions and almost no tourist infrastructure
owens-valley-gunter.hazards: Extreme summer thermals and dust devils on the takeoffs; strong wind along the valley and rotors in the canyons; westerly wind spilling over the Sierra; bushes on the takeoffs snag lines; remote desert landings; Bishop airport airspace
owens-valley-gunter.crowd_note: Few pilots, plenty of room in the air
owens-valley-gunter.region: Bishop, Owens Valley, eastern California (White Mountains / Sierra Nevada)
owens-valley-gunter.season: Spring — May to early June, and autumn — September to mid-October; at the height of summer (July–August) the desert floor overheats and turbulence is extreme — for very experienced pilots only; hardly any flying in winter
owens-valley-gunter.transfer: ~3.5 h from Reno in a rented 4×4; ~4–5 h from Los Angeles / Ontario; Bishop has a small airport
owens-valley-gunter.takeoffs: In the White Mountains above Bishop: Gunter (~2,400 m) and Paiute (~2,420 m) — west-facing daytime takeoffs with 4×4 access; Flynn's (~1,500 m) — easier access, good XC; on the Sierra side near Lone Pine, Walt's Point (~2,740 m), more of a hang gliding takeoff, where the record flights began
owens-valley-gunter.wind_note: Mountain desert thermals: you need light background wind. Along the valley floor there can be strong wind and powerful rotors behind spurs and in the canyons; strong westerly wind can spill over the Sierra crests. Dust devils on the takeoffs — launch in a lull
owens-valley-gunter.best_time: Launches in the middle of the day; thermals roughly from 10:00 to 18:00; in summer, extreme turbulence during the day
owens-valley-gunter.access: Gunter, Paiute and Flynn's — dirt roads, 4×4 only (the road to Paiute is very rough); you can drive up to the hang gliding takeoffs
owens-valley-gunter.xc_note: Cloud base 4,000–6,000 m; the first 100- and 200-mile flights in the US (on paragliders and hang gliders) were launched from Walt's Point; from Walt's it's ~60 miles to Bishop and ~100 to Nevada; from the White Mountains north to the Nevada border ~60 km; from Paiute, flights are usually ~30 miles, plus out-and-returns
owens-valley-gunter.rules: Bishop airport (class E airspace) is a couple of miles east of town — take it into account when flying. The sites are for experienced pilots with mountain experience only
owens-valley-gunter.landing: The valley floor (~1,220 m) — fields and desert near Bishop; along XC routes, desert landings far from roads
owens-valley-gunter.events: Historic records: the first 100- and 200-mile flights in the US were launched from Walt's Point
pros: Cloud base 4,000–6,000 m
XC flights of hundreds of kilometres
Hardly anyone around
The Sierra, Mount Whitney and the desert below you
cons: Extreme turbulence in summer
Difficult 4×4 access
Experienced pilots only, almost no tandems
Far from major airports
owens-valley-gunter.airport: RNO — Reno, ~3.5 h; ONT/LAX — Los Angeles, ~4–5 h
school_notes: Three-time women's hang gliding world champion based in Bishop: courses and guiding
XC tours and clinics in the Owens Valley

point-of-the-mountain-utah.description: Point of the Mountain is a low ridge on the border between the Salt Lake and Utah valleys, where people have been flying for over a century: a smooth southerly wind on the South Side in the morning, a northerly on the North Side in the evening. Thanks to its reliable soaring it's one of the world's main training sites and home to several well-known schools.
point-of-the-mountain-utah.rating_basis: One of the world's best-known training sites: reliable laminar soaring morning and evening, a state park with infrastructure and lots of schools; limited XC potential
point-of-the-mountain-utah.hazards: Wind picking up by mid-morning on the South Side; turbulence when the wind switches around midday; heavy student traffic — follow the right-of-way rules (the pilot with the ridge on their right has priority)
point-of-the-mountain-utah.crowd_note: Lots of students and tandems, especially in the morning on the South Side; queuing rules and flags apply
point-of-the-mountain-utah.region: Draper, between Salt Lake City and Provo, Utah
point-of-the-mountain-utah.season: Flyable year-round: the South Side in the morning, the North Side in the evening; best season April–October; in winter it's cold, with inversions and snow at times, but people fly on clear days too
point-of-the-mountain-utah.transfer: ~30 minutes from Salt Lake City airport on I-15; ~30 minutes from Provo
point-of-the-mountain-utah.takeoffs: South Side — the Flight Park State Recreation Area: morning soaring in southerly wind; North Side — a Salt Lake County park ~2 km to the north: a steeper, higher slope, evening soaring in northerly wind, from where you can “bench up” onto the ridge and cross the valley to the Wasatch
point-of-the-mountain-utah.wind_note: In the morning the valley heats up and the wind draws in from the south towards the mountain, so the South Side works (from ~6:00 until mid-morning, when the wind gets too strong); around midday the wind switches, and pilots move to the North Side for the evening northerly. South Side limits: P2 up to 15 mph, P3 up to 18 mph
point-of-the-mountain-utah.best_time: South Side — from dawn until ~10–11 am (in summer, arrive by 7:30); North Side — in the evening, in summer from 17:00 until sunset
point-of-the-mountain-utah.access: Right by I-15 in Draper: the South Side takeoff is by the state park car park (a Utah State Parks day pass is required), with a campground; the North Side is the neighbouring county park
point-of-the-mountain-utah.xc_note: Mostly soaring along the ridge; on good days pilots climb out from the North Side above the ~3 km ridge and cross the valley to the Wasatch Range
point-of-the-mountain-utah.rules: A USHPA rating is required (foreigners can get USHPA visitor membership based on their IPPI card); students fly only with a certified instructor. UHGPGA rules: launch from the “launch zone” only when the green flag is up; under a red flag, no students (H3/P3+ recommended); helmets mandatory; motors banned; paragliders land west of the centre flag. Utah State Parks rules apply
point-of-the-mountain-utah.landing: Top landing by the takeoff (if it's too windy on top, slide down the slope and land lower) and the landing field at the foot of the South Side; on the South Side there are separate areas for hang gliders (east of the centre flag) and paragliders (west of it)
pros: Two slopes for different winds — fly morning and evening
An excellent place for training and ground handling
Close to Salt Lake City and the airport
Several schools, rental, campground
cons: Crowded
Strong wind and turbulence in the middle of the day, a break in flying
Limited XC opportunities
Expensive tandems
point-of-the-mountain-utah.tandem_price_note: POTMP price list (year not given on the website): morning South Side tandem $225 (20–30 min), evening North Side $275 (30–45 min)
school_notes: School since 1998, tandems and training at Point of the Mountain
Tandems on the South and North Side, P2 course, tours to Valle de Bravo
School and shop by the takeoff

torrey-pines-gliderport.description: Torrey Pines is a legendary gliderport on the La Jolla cliffs above Black's Beach: people were already soaring here in 1930, and today paragliders, hang gliders and model gliders fly the sea breeze. Tandems and training on site, and a steady westerly more than 300 days a year.
torrey-pines-gliderport.rating_basis: A famous historic US coastal soaring spot: 300+ flyable days, flights over ocean cliffs, an official gliderport with a school and rental; of no interest to XC pilots
torrey-pines-gliderport.hazards: Top landing near the cliff edge takes skill; if the wind drops, you land on the beach and walk back up; heavy traffic on the ridge (paragliders, hang gliders, models); fog and low cloud from spring into early summer
torrey-pines-gliderport.crowd_note: At weekends, lots of pilots, tandems, radio-controlled gliders and spectators; heavy traffic on the short stretch of ridge
torrey-pines-gliderport.season: Flyable year-round — more than 300 flyable days; from spring to autumn a long flying window from morning to evening, in winter a shorter window (11:00–16:00), with more rain and easterly winds
torrey-pines-gliderport.transfer: ~25 minutes by car from San Diego airport; public transport to the gliderport is inconvenient
torrey-pines-gliderport.wind_note: Classic ridge soaring over ~100-metre cliffs by Black's Beach in a 240–280° westerly sea breeze: paragliders need ~7–15 mph (11–24 km/h), hang gliders 10–18 mph
torrey-pines-gliderport.best_time: In autumn and winter it's usually flyable roughly from 11:00 to 16:00, in spring and summer from 9:00 to 19:00; the gliderport is open from 9:00 until sunset
torrey-pines-gliderport.access: Takeoff and landing are right by the gliderport car park (Torrey Pines Scenic Dr), next to the Cliff Hanger café; 25 minutes from downtown San Diego
torrey-pines-gliderport.xc_note: Almost no XC — soaring along the cliffs above the La Jolla coast and Black's Beach
torrey-pines-gliderport.rules: To fly solo — USHPA P3 with 50 hours of airtime (hang gliders H4); P2 pilots only under instructor supervision. Foreigners need an equivalent level on their IPPI card (Para Pro 4, ~150 flights, 50 hours) and a ground handling check with an instructor. Mandatory registration at the office, a waiver, a video briefing, a whistle and a radio receiving 151.505 MHz; fee $10 a day or $200 a year
torrey-pines-gliderport.landing: Landing back on top of the cliff by the takeoff (top landing); in light wind, on Black's Beach below, followed by a ~15-minute hike up the cliff
torrey-pines-gliderport.events: A historic gliderport since 1930 (Charles Lindbergh made the first flight over the cliffs); a National Landmark of Soaring and listed on the US National Register of Historic Places
pros: Laminar sea breeze more than 300 days a year
Takeoff and landing by the car park, café on site
Official school, rental and walk-in tandems
Beautiful views of the ocean and La Jolla
cons: Strict entry requirements: P3 and 50 hours of airtime
Expensive tandems
No XC
Crowded at weekends
torrey-pines-gliderport.tandem_price_note: Paragliding tandem of ~20 minutes, $190 cash; no advance booking — first come, first served, weather permitting; photos/video extra. Hang gliding tandems are temporarily unavailable
school_notes: The gliderport's official concessionaire: tandems, training, rental, sign-off for visiting pilots

chimgan-amirsoy-charvak.description: The Charvak reservoir in Bostanliq District is Uzbekistan's main paragliding site: from a flying site on the shore, operators run short tandems over the water, while the summit of the Amirsoy resort (2,290 m, gondola), Lesser Chimgan and Beldersay offer longer flights from the mountains with a landing by Charvak. It's all 1.5 hours from Tashkent, and the operators speak Russian.
chimgan-amirsoy-charvak.rating_basis: Uzbekistan's main flying site: tandems over Charvak 1.5 h from Tashkent, a takeoff from the Amirsoy gondola and hike & fly from Lesser Chimgan; little information for visiting pilots and no data on XC flights
chimgan-amirsoy-charvak.hazards: Strong thermals and heat in June–August, mountain-valley winds, helicopter traffic over Charvak and Amirsoy, landing by the water
chimgan-amirsoy-charvak.crowd_note: No data on crowds; flights are mostly tandems for tourists from Tashkent
chimgan-amirsoy-charvak.region: Bostanliq District, Tashkent Region, Western Tien Shan, shore of the Charvak reservoir, 60–80 km from Tashkent
chimgan-amirsoy-charvak.season: Late March / early April to mid-October (until the autumn rains); best May–September; thermals peak in June–August
chimgan-amirsoy-charvak.transfer: 60–80 km from Tashkent, ~1.5 h by car; suburban train to Khojikent station, then a taxi along Charvak
chimgan-amirsoy-charvak.takeoffs: The point on the map is the paragliding base (flying site) on the shore of Charvak by the R-12 highway: short tandems over the reservoir and training flights in ridge lift; takeoff altitude not published. Other takeoffs: the summit of the Amirsoy resort (2,290 m, gondola) — an XC tandem of ~25 km to Charvak; Lesser Chimgan (~2,098 m, hike up via the Pesochny Pass) — a 10–15 km flight to Charvak; Beldersay — the chairlift top station (~2,100 m) on Mount Kumbel, thermal flights
chimgan-amirsoy-charvak.wind_note: Flights depend on wind strength and direction — sometimes you have to wait for the weather; at Charvak people fly in ridge lift on the shore slope, from the mountains (Beldersay, Amirsoy, Lesser Chimgan) on daytime thermals; according to the operators, the wind direction is steady through the day and the season
chimgan-amirsoy-charvak.best_time: Tandems roughly from 11:30 to 16:00; the strongest thermals and heat are from early June to late August
chimgan-amirsoy-charvak.access: The Charvak flying site — ~1.5 h by car from Tashkent (or by train to Khojikent and then a taxi); Amirsoy — gondola up to 2,290 m; Lesser Chimgan — a 3.5 km hike with ~550 m of ascent; in Beldersay, the chairlift up Kumbel
chimgan-amirsoy-charvak.xc_note: XC tandems from Amirsoy to Charvak, ~25 km (45–90 minutes), and from Lesser Chimgan, 10–15 km; pilot programmes include trial XC flights from Beldersay to the Charvak shore. No data on records or XContest flights could be found
chimgan-amirsoy-charvak.rules: Paragliders give way to helicopters: a flight may be delayed for several hours or cancelled on the controller's orders. Tandem passengers must be at least 5 years old and weigh at least 30 kg (Paraplan uz). A pilot programme (2012 data) required a course completion certificate and your own gear, with rental by arrangement. Russians don't need a visa
chimgan-amirsoy-charvak.landing: Landing on the shore of the Charvak reservoir by the flying site — after a flight from Amirsoy, operators describe it as “soft”
chimgan-amirsoy-charvak.events: The Uzbekistan Paragliding Championship “Chimgan Air Battle 2018” (planned for summer 2018)
pros: 1.5 hours from Tashkent
Views of Charvak and the Western Tien Shan
Takeoff from the Amirsoy gondola and hike & fly from Lesser Chimgan
Russian-speaking operators
cons: Short tandems (7–15 minutes) at the base price
Helicopters have priority — delays and cancellations possible
Little information for visiting pilots
chimgan-amirsoy-charvak.tandem_price_note: Paraplan uz over Charvak (Afisha.uz, September 2026): 7–8 min — 700,000 som, 12–15 min — 1,000,000, 18–20 min — 1,200,000, 30 min — 1,500,000, GoPro video +100,000. GoFLY — from 800,000 som, Travel Ornament — $70 for 10 min (2026). An XC tandem from Amirsoy (45–90 min) with People Travel — from $360 in a package with transfer from Tashkent
school_notes: Tandems over Charvak from 7 to 30 minutes, 700,000–1,500,000 som (2026), booking via Telegram
Tandem with a trip from Tashkent, $120 per person, in Russian (English on request)
Tashkent agency: tandem over Charvak, hike & fly from Lesser Chimgan and an XC flight from Amirsoy (~25 km) with transfer
Short tandem over Charvak, $70 for 10 minutes; season from late March to mid-October

khau-pha-mu-cang-chai.description: Khau Pha Pass is one of the “four great passes” of northern Vietnam and the country's main tandem takeoff: a flight over the terraced rice fields of the Cao Pha valley in Mu Cang Chai. The most beautiful months are September, when the rice turns golden, and the spring “water season”, when the terraces are flooded; paragliding festivals are held during these periods.
khau-pha-mu-cang-chai.rating_basis: Vietnam's best-known tandem site (festivals, “Top 7 experiences in Vietnam” 2023), ~2,000 passengers a year; for pilots, limited access and short flights
khau-pha-mu-cang-chai.hazards: Mountain turbulence near takeoff, landing on terraces, fog and thunderstorms in the rainy season
khau-pha-mu-cang-chai.crowd_note: Queues at weekends and on festival days in the golden season; at the peak, 15–20 tandem pilots are working
khau-pha-mu-cang-chai.region: Mu Cang Chai, Lao Cai Province (formerly Yen Bai), north-western Vietnam
khau-pha-mu-cang-chai.season: tandem seasons follow the rice fields: the “water season” in April–June and the “golden season” from late August to November (best in September); fog and cold in winter, rainy season in July
khau-pha-mu-cang-chai.transfer: About 5 h from Hanoi (Hanoi–Lao Cai expressway, then via Nghia Lo); the nearest town is Mu Cang Chai
khau-pha-mu-cang-chai.wind_note: A mountain takeoff at the highest point of the pass above the Cao Pha valley; there's no reliable data on the workable wind directions — the operator runs flights when conditions are suitable
khau-pha-mu-cang-chai.best_time: Tandems during the day; flights of 10–25 minutes, about 3 km in a straight line to the landing field in the valley
khau-pha-mu-cang-chai.access: The takeoff is by the road at the top of Khau Pha Pass (the Nghia Lo–Mu Cang Chai road), with a café overlooking the takeoff; about 5 h by car from Hanoi
khau-pha-mu-cang-chai.xc_note: Mostly tandem flights over the rice terraces; the mountains have XC potential, but flying is limited by airspace permits
khau-pha-mu-cang-chai.rules: Flying in Vietnam requires an airspace use permit from the General Staff (Operations Department) of the Vietnam People's Army; foreign pilots fly only through local clubs and the operator (Viên Nam / Mebayluon, the Vietwings Hanoi club); tandems are run by a single contractor under an agreement with the local authorities until the end of 2026
khau-pha-mu-cang-chai.landing: Landing in the Lim Mong valley (Cao Pha commune) among the rice terraces; the landing field was repaired after floods (2026)
khau-pha-mu-cang-chai.events: The festivals “Flying over the golden season” (Bay trên mùa vàng, late August–September) and “Flying over the water season” (Bay trên mùa nước đổ, April–June), with up to 100–200 pilots
pros: Incredible views of the rice terraces
Festivals with hundreds of pilots
Tandem with insurance included in the price
cons: Far from Hanoi
Short seasons that depend on the rice and the weather
Difficult access for independent pilots (military permits)
Short flights
khau-pha-mu-cang-chai.tandem_price_note: Tandem with insurance; prices are higher on festival days
school_notes: The main tandem operator at Khau Pha
Hanoi club that organises the festivals; flights for pilots go through it

cape-town-signal-hill.description: Signal Hill is a ridge above Sea Point in central Cape Town: tandems launch by the car park at the top, soar with views of Table Mountain, Lion's Head and the Atlantic, and land on the promenade lawn. For pilots it's a sporty ridge-soaring takeoff with gusty wind, open only to experienced pilots under local supervision.
cape-town-signal-hill.rating_basis: One of the world's most spectacular urban tandems — views of Table Mountain, Lion's Head and the Atlantic, landing on the promenade; for pilots, a tricky Sport-rated takeoff
cape-town-signal-hill.hazards: Wind gradient and sudden strengthening of the NW wind, berg wind, turbulence in S and SW wind, an outlanding among the buildings of Green Point, venturi between the Twelve Apostles when crossing to Lion's Head
cape-town-signal-hill.crowd_note: On good days, a queue of tandems by the car park and lots of wings in the narrow corridor above Sea Point
cape-town-signal-hill.season: year-round on days with a NW or westerly breeze; best in autumn (March–April) and spring (October–November); at the height of summer a strong south-easterly often gets in the way, in winter fronts and rain
cape-town-signal-hill.transfer: ~25–30 minutes from Cape Town airport to Signal Hill; 10–15 minutes from the centre and Sea Point
cape-town-signal-hill.takeoffs: Signal Hill: the takeoff by the car park (green mat, for NW wind) and The Bench, 500 m further south along the ridge — for strong westerlies; tandems fly from the takeoffs on Lion's Head when the wind suits; in light wind, Sir Lowry's Pass
cape-town-signal-hill.wind_note: Ridge lift in NW (best) and westerly wind of up to 35 km/h; avoid the hot, gusty berg wind (NE) and the period just after the wind switches from NE to NW; SW at The Bench is very turbulent; strong southerlies cause turbulence below 100 m; the summer south-easter (the “Cape Doctor”) blows from behind
cape-town-signal-hill.best_time: Tandems on any flyable day; you often wait for the breeze to fill in; for pilots, the classic is Sunday afternoon soaring
cape-town-signal-hill.access: By car via Kloof Nek Road and Signal Hill Road to the car park at the top — the takeoff is next to the car park
cape-town-signal-hill.xc_note: Signal Hill itself is ridge soaring with a 1,200 m airspace ceiling and a crossing to Lion's Head; for XC, pilots head to Porterville (~2 h north, season December–January)
cape-town-signal-hill.rules: The takeoff is for Sport-rated pilots only (IPPI 5+); all pilots must be SAHPA members with an SACAA licence; foreigners need a SAHPA Foreign Pilot Permit and may fly only under the supervision of a Sport-rated pilot or instructor; a first-flight briefing is mandatory, as is a SANParks “My Activity” permit (level 2) for Table Mountain National Park — a day permit can be bought from the tandem pilots on takeoff; training beginners on Signal Hill is banned; ceiling 1,200 m
cape-town-signal-hill.landing: The Sea Point promenade lawn opposite the Winchester Mansions hotel; in southerly wind, the fields by the stadium (strong rotor); don't glide low towards Green Point — you'd end up outlanding among buildings
pros: Incredible views of Table Mountain and the ocean
Drive right up to takeoff
Landing on the promenade in the city centre
cons: Gusty wind, a Sport-rated site
Foreign pilots need permits and may fly only under supervision
Short tandems in light wind
Queues in season
cape-town-signal-hill.tandem_price_note: 5–20 minutes in the air depending on the wind; Para-Taxi from 1,500 ZAR + GoPro video 300 ZAR; the sources don't give the price year — probably 2025
school_notes: Tandems from Signal Hill
Tandems from Signal Hill and Lion's Head, also Sir Lowry's Pass and Hermanus
Basic licence courses (~14 days)
Pilot training

geraldton-coronation-beach.description: Coronation Beach near Geraldton is one of Western Australia's windiest and most famous windsurf spots: from November to March a 20–30-knot side-shore sea breeze blows almost every afternoon. The shallow, standing-depth lagoon by the shore suits learning, freeriding and first jumps, while the outer reef offers waves for bump & jump and wave riding. There's a basic campground right by the beach, and Geraldton has another dozen spots (Sunset Beach, Point Moore, Hell's Gate).
geraldton-coronation-beach.rating_basis: Surf Magazin (the best wind statistics in Western Australia), Visit Geraldton (“one of the best places in the world for jumping”), Tourism WA and Kiteforum: a near-daily 20+ knot breeze, a standing-depth lagoon for learning and reef waves; downsides — remoteness, little rental, no water on site
geraldton-coronation-beach.waves_note: The first ~800 m from shore is a shallow, mostly standing-depth lagoon with flat water, light chop and the occasional clean waist-high wave (ideal for first jumps and loops). On the outer reef and sandbar — 1–4 m waves: depending on the swell, anything from “a bad day on the Baltic” to “a good day on Tenerife”; far out it gets dangerous in big swells
geraldton-coronation-beach.hazards: Reefs and rocks; dangerous waves on the outer reef in big swells, and no rescue service — if you break gear, you swim to shore; collisions with kiters (stay in your zone); sharks (this is Western Australia); strong sun; a dangerous downhill stretch on the access road
geraldton-coronation-beach.gustiness_note: In the morning usually offshore and lighter (~15 knots); by lunchtime the 20–30-knot sea breeze sets in and holds until dark; one of the windiest spots in Western Australia
geraldton-coronation-beach.crowd_note: A popular spot — in season you'll rarely have the water to yourself, and the campground is often full in summer; but there's plenty of room in the lagoon and on the reef
geraldton-coronation-beach.region: Western Australia, ~30 km north of Geraldton (Howatharra)
geraldton-coronation-beach.events: Wave Rally World Championships — figure-of-eight races on wave gear through the lagoon and the surf, based at the Geraldton Windsurfing Club (January; next edition 6–10 January 2027)
geraldton-coronation-beach.launch: Sandy beach by the campground and car park (toilets, barbecues, lookout); windsurfers launch south of the car park, kiters in the northern part (kite zone 300 m downwind). No drinking water or electricity on site — the nearest water is at a petrol station 15 km away
geraldton-coronation-beach.sail_note: Usually 4.2–5.3 m² (typically around 4.7), 3.7–4.2 on strong days; 5.5–6.5 in the mornings and on light days
pros: One of the best wind statistics in Western Australia
Standing-depth lagoon and reef waves in one place
A great place for jumps and loops
Campground right on the beach, and a town nearby with spots for every wind direction
cons: No schools or proper rental — better bring your own gear
No water or electricity on site
Far from Perth, you need a car
Cool water in spring (~19 °C)
geraldton-coronation-beach.wind_dir: S–SW (sea breeze), side-shore; in the evening it veers slightly side-off
geraldton-coronation-beach.airport: GET — Geraldton, ~30 km (about 30 minutes); PER — Perth, ~430 km (4.5–5 hours)
school_notes: Private rental of basic windsurf kits (for confident riders) with delivery around Geraldton, plus camping gear and a caravan (Seabreeze listing, 2023)

gnaraloo.description: Gnaraloo is a remote pastoral station on the Ningaloo coast, where windsurfers from all over the world come for Tombstones — a long left-hand reef wave that a strong 25–30-knot side-shore breeze “switches on” in season. This is a place for experienced wave sailors: launching off the reef, side-off wind, no services, and accommodation at the 3 Mile campground. For a break from the waves there's flat water nearby in Gnaraloo Bay.
gnaraloo.rating_basis: Surf Magazin (Western Australia spot guide), Boards (“Epic Gnaraloo”), Severne and Seabreeze: one of the best windsurf waves in the world — a long, predictable left in a steady, strong breeze; downsides — extreme remoteness, no rental or services, sharp reef
gnaraloo.waves_note: Tombstones is a long, predictable, world-class left-hand reef wave (up to 15+ turns per ride); it works from 1.5–2 m, holds 4 m+ and is best in a big W / SW swell. After the ride you're flushed into the lagoon inside the reef, where the wave dies out. Flat water for freeriding is in Gnaraloo Bay a few kilometres north and in the bay by the shearing shed
gnaraloo.hazards: Sharp, shallow reef and sea urchins (booties are a must), especially at low tide; powerful, heavy waves and currents; side-offshore wind — if you break gear, you get blown out; sharks (tiger and bronze whaler) — this is Western Australia; heat and sun; remoteness — help is far away and there's often no phone signal
gnaraloo.gustiness_note: A strong summer breeze blows almost every day from late November to late February, usually 25–30 knots; it often picks up only after 14:00. The wind is side-off — there can be holes near the shore and behind the ledge
gnaraloo.crowd_note: On a good day up to 20–25 windsurfers and kiters on the wave, plus surfers in the morning; empty the rest of the time
gnaraloo.region: Western Australia, Gnaraloo Station (3 Mile campground), ~150 km north of Carnarvon
gnaraloo.launch: Launch from a small bay upwind of the wave, a few minutes from the 3 Mile campground; to reach the water you climb down a low (~2 m) ledge and cross the reef. At low tide you have to bear away sharply downwind right after launching to avoid being washed onto the reef. Booties are a must. No rental, lifeguards or shade
gnaraloo.sail_note: 4.2–4.7 m² in the main season (for ~75 kg), 5.0–5.5 on lighter days; 5–6 m² for freeriding in the bay
pros: World-class wave — a long, predictable left
Strong breeze almost daily from late November to February
Few people, wild nature (turtles, Ningaloo reefs)
Flat water nearby for freeride and freestyle
cons: Very remote: 12+ hours from Perth, the last 80 km on a dirt road
No rental, schools or shops (just a small shop at the campground)
Sharp reef and side-off wind — for experienced sailors only
Heat, flies, no shade or drinking water
gnaraloo.airport: CVQ — Carnarvon, ~150 km (about 2 hours, the last ~80 km on a dirt road); PER — Perth, ~1,100–1,200 km (12+ hours by car)

lancelin-windsurf.description: Lancelin is Western Australia's legendary windsurf town: from November to March a 20+ knot southerly sea breeze blows almost every day. The bay behind the reef forms a shallow, flat-water lagoon for learning, freestyle and speed, while the reef spots Main Break and South Passage offer quality left-hand waves. Since 1986 the town has hosted the Lancelin Ocean Classic, with wave contests and the Ledge Point → Lancelin marathon.
lancelin-windsurf.rating_basis: Boards, Windsurf Magazine, Seabreeze and Big Salty: Western Australia's “windsurf capital” — a reliable 20+ knot summer breeze, a flat lagoon for learning and freestyle right next to reef waves, and the long-running Lancelin Ocean Classic. Downsides — remoteness, little rental, cool water in spring
lancelin-windsurf.waves_note: Inside the bay, sheltered by a reef ~500 m offshore, the water is flat and shallow near the beach. Waves on the reefs: Main Break (punchy lefts right at the lagoon exit), South Passage (long, powerful lefts ~1 km offshore, for experienced sailors), and Back Beach beyond the point — shorebreak with no reef. The best swells come in October–November and March–April
lancelin-windsurf.hazards: Shallow reef in the lagoon at low tide; at Main Break, if you go too far upwind you get washed onto the reef; at South Passage, rocks and Lancelin Island across the passage, big waves and a long swim to shore; sharks (this is Western Australia); very strong sun
lancelin-windsurf.gustiness_note: The summer sea breeze (the “Fremantle Doctor”) blows on 70–80% of days, averaging 20–22 knots; it picks up by 10–12 o'clock and holds until dark. The wind is steady and stronger than in Perth
lancelin-windsurf.crowd_note: In summer (especially in January and on public holidays) there are lots of windsurfers and kiters at Main Break and in the lagoon; kiters are advised to launch closer to the point, away from the windsurf zone and the swimming beach
lancelin-windsurf.region: Western Australia, ~130 km north of Perth
lancelin-windsurf.events: Lancelin Ocean Classic — Australia's biggest windsurf festival, held in January since 1986: reef wave sailing, slalom and a 20–25 km Ledge Point → Lancelin marathon (together with kiters); it returned in 2019 after a break
lancelin-windsurf.launch: The main launch is the grassy rigging area by the car park in front of the campground (Grace Darling Park, the “windsurf park”): toilets, showers, a sandy beach and shallow water near the shore — handy for beginners. For Main Break you sail out of the lagoon downwind through the gap in the reef; for South Passage you launch from the Jetty in the northern part of town
lancelin-windsurf.sail_note: Usually 4.5–5.8 m², around 5.2 on a good day; 4.0–4.7 on the wave in a strong breeze. On light days and for the marathon — race sails of 7–8.6 m²
pros: Reliable summer breeze almost every day
Flat lagoon and reef waves in one place
Convenient grassy rigging area with showers and toilets
Ledge Point, Wedge Island, Cervantes and the Lancelin dunes nearby
cons: A long flight, and you need a car
Minimal rental, better bring your own gear
Cool water in spring (19–20 °C), you need a shorty wetsuit
Strong sun and heat
lancelin-windsurf.wind_dir: S–SSW (sea breeze), often offshore in the morning, side-onshore from the left during the day
lancelin-windsurf.airport: PER — Perth, ~130 km (1.5–2 hours by car)
school_notes: Rental and lessons from a trailer on the main beach (Starboard / Severne), season October–April, book 24 hours ahead, cash only; no recent confirmation that it's still operating — check in advance

aruba-fishermans-huts-windsurf.description: Fisherman's Huts (Hadicurari Beach) is Aruba's main windsurf beach, at the northern end of Palm Beach. A strong north-easterly trade wind blows almost all year round, and the water is shallow and wave-free, making it a slalom and freestyle classic. Multiple freestyle world champion Sarah-Quita Offringa sails here too. The Aruba Hi-Winds contest has been held on this beach since 1987. The strongest wind is from May to July.
aruba-fishermans-huts-windsurf.rating_basis: Aruba's most popular windsurf beach. The PWA calls it a “legendary slalom venue”, and Aruba Hi-Winds has been held here since 1987. A strong trade wind about 350 days a year and shallow water; the downside is the gusty offshore wind
aruba-fishermans-huts-windsurf.waves_note: No waves: this is the island's lee shore. Shallow water with moderate chop, smooth near the beach
aruba-fishermans-huts-windsurf.hazards: Offshore wind: if you break gear or the wind drops, you get blown away from shore. Rocks and pebbles at the entry, kiters, fishing boats
aruba-fishermans-huts-windsurf.gustiness_note: The trade wind crosses the island and is a little gusty near the shore (offshore wind). It's steadier further out
aruba-fishermans-huts-windsurf.crowd_note: Several schools and kiters on the beach. Busy in season and during Hi-Winds, but there's plenty of water
aruba-fishermans-huts-windsurf.region: Northwest coast, between Palm Beach and Malmok
aruba-fishermans-huts-windsurf.events: Aruba Hi-Winds — an annual windsurf contest since 1987 (June–July). In 2025 (28 May – 2 June) the beach hosted the PWA Youth Slalom Championship on fin and foil
aruba-fishermans-huts-windsurf.launch: White sand with pebbles and rocks, next to the fishermen's huts and the centres (Vela is in a two-storey building behind the Ritz-Carlton). Shallow for more than 60 m from shore. Minimal current. Water shoes come in handy
aruba-fishermans-huts-windsurf.sail_note: Usually 4.7–5.7 m², 4.2–4.7 on strong days in May–July; 6.0–7.5 or foil in the lighter months (September–November)
pros: Strong trade wind about 350 days a year
Shallow water near the shore, good for both beginners and slalom sailors
Warm water and a dry climate, outside the hurricane belt
Convenient centres, hotels and restaurants nearby
cons: Offshore wind: gusty near the beach, and if you break gear you get blown out to sea
Rocks and pebbles at the shore
Expensive resort
Noticeably lighter wind in September–November
aruba-fishermans-huts-windsurf.wind_dir: E–ENE trade wind, side-off / offshore from the left
school_notes: windsurf and kite school right at Fisherman's Huts, with a second base on Palm Beach
windsurf lessons and rental, recommended for beginners

bonaire-lac-bay.description: Lac Bay is a huge shallow lagoon on the east side of Bonaire, sheltered by a reef. A steady trade wind blows in from the sea across the reef, and in the southern part the water is waist-deep or less. This is the “spiritual home of freestyle”: many top freestylers grew up here, and PWA events have been held here. It's the easiest place for beginners, while pros come to work on their tricks. Kites are banned; the best wind is from December to August.
bonaire-lac-bay.rating_basis: One of the world's best shallow flat-water spots (Surf Magazin, Carib Journal). It has hosted PWA freestyle events and is home to freestyle stars (the Frans brothers and others). Steady trade wind, kites banned
bonaire-lac-bay.waves_note: The water in the lagoon is smooth, with light chop in the deeper “blue” part for freestyle and slalom. Beyond the reef at the mouth of the bay there are waves for jumping on good days
bonaire-lac-bay.hazards: A sudden drop-off in the northern part of the lagoon, open sea and current beyond the reef, fragile mangroves and seagrass (stay within the marked zones), strong sun
bonaire-lac-bay.gustiness_note: The trade wind passes over the flat reef and blows steadily into the lagoon. Strongest from 11:00 to 15:00, easing off towards evening
bonaire-lac-bay.crowd_note: Kiting is banned in Lac Bay: only windsurfers, wing foilers and SUPs on the water. The lagoon is large (about 700 ha), but it can get busy near the centres in season
bonaire-lac-bay.events: PWA Freestyle World Cup events. The most recent one described in the sources, the Forsa Bonaire PWA World Cup, was held on 9–13 April 2019 at Jibe City. The PWA calls Bonaire the “spiritual home of freestyle”
bonaire-lac-bay.launch: Sorobon sandy beach, with centres and bars right on the shore and rigged sails waiting on racks. In the southern part of the lagoon in front of Jibe City the depth averages about 80 cm, max about 1.2 m, over fine sand with no coral. The northern part drops off sharply into deep water (you can tell by the dark colour). You need the annual STINAPA nature fee ($40, available at the centres)
bonaire-lac-bay.sail_note: Most people use 4.7 and 5.4 m²; freestylers 4.2–5.7. 6.0–7.0 in the lighter months (September–November)
pros: Shallow flat water with a sandy bottom, you can stand almost everywhere
Steady trade wind, an 8–9-month windy season
Kites banned, plenty of room on the water
Excellent centres and schools, warm water
Ideal for learning and freestyle
cons: Hardly any waves
Light wind in September–November
Expensive destination, you need a car
Mandatory STINAPA nature fee
bonaire-lac-bay.wind_dir: E trade wind, side-onshore (from the sea across the reef into the lagoon)
bonaire-lac-bay.rental_price_note: per day of rental; about $490 for a week (10–15% discount), according to the Bonaire.com guide
school_notes: the main centre in the southern part of the lagoon: 170 boards and 150+ rigged sails, lessons from $50, Hang Out bar
lessons from $50, freestyle; instructors include PWA freestyler Youp Schmit
rental and lessons on Sorobon beach

ilha-do-guajiru.description: Ilha do Guajiru is a village of a dozen pousadas on a sand spit near Itarema, between Fortaleza and Jericoacoara. It has a large, shallow flat-water lagoon, and from July to January a thermally boosted trade wind blows almost every day. It's primarily a kite spot, but conditions for freeride, freestyle and foil windsurfing are excellent too. Handy to stop off with your own gear on the way to or from Jeri.
ilha-do-guajiru.rating_basis: A well-known kite spot: Ceará's largest flat-water lagoon with reliable wind from July to January. Spot guides note that it suits windsurfing too. Rating lowered for the lack of windsurf infrastructure, the shallows at low tide and the wind shadow near the shore
ilha-do-guajiru.waves_note: Flat water or light chop in the lagoon. Small waves only outside, on the ocean side of the spit (at low tide you can walk there via a sandy islet)
ilha-do-guajiru.hazards: Shallows at low tide. Sharp shells on the bottom in places: wear shoes. Boats and fishermen's moorings in the lagoon. Gusts and wind shadow near the shore, slippery sand at low tide, strong sun
ilha-do-guajiru.gustiness_note: A trade wind boosted by the daytime thermal. In the lagoon the wind is gustier than on the ocean, especially near the built-up shore. Locals say the real wind is often 2–5 knots stronger than forecast
ilha-do-guajiru.crowd_note: Few windsurfers — the water is mostly full of kiters, especially by the pousadas. The lagoon is big, so there's room if you move downwind. Busy during GKA kite freestyle events (the World Championship final was also held here, in October)
ilha-do-guajiru.launch: Launch from the beach in front of the pousadas on the Guajiru spit, straight into the lagoon. The lagoon is large (about 5 km²) and shallow; at low tide it gets noticeably shallower and narrower and the beach becomes wide. Best sailed at high tide. At full high tide there's a wind shadow by the pousadas, so people launch a 5-minute walk upwind or downwind. At low tide the wet sand is very slippery
ilha-do-guajiru.sail_note: Usually 4.7–5.8 m² from August to November, 5.5–6.5 in July, December and January. Boards of 90–105 l suit flat-water freestyle
pros: Huge flat-water lagoon with standing depth
Wind almost every day from August to December
Warm water all year round
Quiet village, accommodation right on the shore
cons: No windsurf centres or rental found, you need your own gear
At low tide the lagoon gets very shallow and the fin can touch the bottom
Wind shadow by the pousadas at high tide
Lots of kiters on the water
Rainy season and light wind from March to May
ilha-do-guajiru.airport: JJD — Jericoacoara (Cruz), ~65 km, about 1.5 hours; or FOR — Fortaleza, ~235 km, 2.5–3 hours

jericoacoara-windsurf.description: Jericoacoara (Jeri) is a village among the dunes in northern Ceará and one of Brazil's top windsurf spots. From July to January a thermally boosted trade wind blows almost every day, often at 25–35 knots from August to November. At the point in front of Club Ventos there are ramps and swell, in front of the dune there's flat water for freestyle, and upwind lies the Malhada wave spot.
jericoacoara-windsurf.rating_basis: One of South America's best-known windsurf spots (Boards, Windsurf UK, Surf Magazin): wind almost every day from August to November, with both waves and flat water. Rating lowered for the gusts by the point, the current and the crowds
jericoacoara-windsurf.waves_note: The waves depend on the tide. At low tide there are hardly any, just chop. At high tide it's smoother inside the bay, with ramps and big, rounded swell outside. The swell builds from September, with the biggest waves in November (sometimes mast-high). The Malhada wave spot is a few tacks upwind, in front of the rocks
jericoacoara-windsurf.hazards: A constant left-to-right current, up to 6 knots at spring high tide. Shifting rocks by Club Ventos and rocks at Malhada (check them at low tide). Wind shadow at high tide, crowds on the wave, sand parasites (bicho-geográfico) — wear shoes; strong sun
jericoacoara-windsurf.gustiness_note: The thermally boosted trade wind picks up from 10 am and peaks in the afternoon. At high tide there's wind shadow and gusts near the point and the new buildings, and it's gusty downwind in the bay. Forecasts underestimate the wind by 5–10 knots
jericoacoara-windsurf.crowd_note: At the height of the season the wave at the main spot gets crowded. At Malhada windsurfers share the waves with kiters and surfers. Kiters are not allowed to launch from the main beach and go to Preá instead
jericoacoara-windsurf.launch: Launch from the village's main beach by Sunset Dune, in front of Club Ventos. Sand at low and mid tide, pebbles at full high tide, when the water reaches the centre's steps. There are rocks by the centre that shift position: carry your gear along the point and launch away from them. Beyond the first line of breakers you need a waterstart
jericoacoara-windsurf.sail_note: Usually 4.0–4.7 m² from August to November, 3.5–4.0 on strong days; 4.7–5.5 in July, December and January. Boards of 75–95 l
pros: Wind almost every day from August to November
Ramps, waves and flat water in one place
Warm water all year round
Atmospheric village with no tarmac, lagoons nearby
cons: Strong current and gusts by the point
Rainy season and light wind from March to May
Crowded on the water in season
Long journey, the last stretch over sand by 4×4
jericoacoara-windsurf.wind_dir: E–ESE trade wind, side-shore from the right
jericoacoara-windsurf.airport: JJD — Jericoacoara (Cruz), ~40 minutes by 4×4; or FOR — Fortaleza, a ~4–5-hour transfer
jericoacoara-windsurf.rental_price_note: about €515 for 15 days at Jeri250 (2016); Club Ventos is newer and pricier
school_notes: Fabio Nobre's centre by Sunset Dune, right in front of The Point: JP and Starboard boards, NeilPryde sails, courses from beginner to wave
RRD board and sail rental, cheaper than Club Ventos (2016 data)
Tabou and Simmer board rental next to Club Ventos

silvaplana.description: Silvaplana is a lake at about 1,800 m in the Upper Engadine near St. Moritz, famous for the Maloja thermal wind: on sunny days it arrives from the Italian-speaking Val Bregaglia shortly before noon and blows until evening at Force 4–6. Here you'll find the “highest windsurf school”, international regattas and Alpine scenery. The season is short — June to September — and the water is cold.
silvaplana.rating_basis: The best-known high-altitude windsurf spot in the Alps: the Maloja thermal blows on almost every sunny summer day, the “highest windsurf school” (1790 m), international regattas; downsides — a short season and very cold water
silvaplana.waves_note: High-altitude lake (~1790 m): light chop at Silvaplana in strong wind, flat water at Sils (station 2); no waves
silvaplana.hazards: Cold water and rapid hypothermia; sudden weather changes and thunderstorms in the mountains; gusts when the thermal is unstable; lots of wing foilers and kiters on the water
silvaplana.gustiness_note: The Maloja thermal spills over the Maloja Pass from Val Bregaglia: on sunny days it starts shortly before noon, quickly builds to Force 4–5 with gusts up to Force 6 and dies down by evening; cloud cover and a northerly airflow weaken it
silvaplana.crowd_note: On good summer days there are lots of windsurfers, wing foilers and kiters on the water (kiters have their own zone by the Mulets sports centre); beginners and families head to the station in Sils
silvaplana.events: Vanora EngadinWinD — an international regatta; in 2025 the iQFoil International Games, in 2026 on 17–28 August (around 150 athletes from 20 countries)
silvaplana.launch: A south-facing pebble beach in the northern part of the lake by the village; some riders launch from the station's slipway in the small harbour. Station 2 in Sils (Sils Maria): offshore wind and flat water — for beginners, kids and families, with a free shuttle between the stations
silvaplana.sail_note: Usually 5.0–6.0 m² (the air at 1800 m is thin — take a sail one size bigger than at sea), 4.5–4.8 on strong days; 6.5–7.5 or foil in light wind
pros: Reliable thermal on almost every sunny summer day
Flat water and chop — freeride, slalom, freestyle, foil
Beginner zone with flat water at Sils
Stunning Alpine views
cons: Very cold water (10–14 °C) — you need a full wetsuit
Short season: the station runs roughly from late May to September
Expensive Switzerland (rental 110+ CHF a day)
Wind only in the afternoon and only in sunny weather
silvaplana.wind_dir: SW (Maloja), onshore / side-shore at the Silvaplana station, offshore at Sils
silvaplana.airport: ZRH — Zurich, ~3 h; MXP — Milan Malpensa, ~3 h; BGY — Bergamo, ~2 h 45 min; local Samedan airfield (SMV) — 15 minutes
silvaplana.rental_price_note: Windsurfing Silvaplana: freeride kit (board + rig) 110 CHF per day, 120 CHF with wetsuit and harness; beginner kit 80 CHF
school_notes: two stations — Silvaplana (for advanced riders) and Sils (for beginners and kids), rental, courses, foil; 2025 season: 19 May – 21 September, 09:00–17:00

matanzas.description: Matanzas is a fishing village 160 km southwest of Santiago and one of South America's top wave capitals. From October to March the southerly surazo blows along the coast, and the Pacific swell breaks into a fast left for port-tack wave riding. It hosts PWA/IWT World Cup events, and Topocalma, Pupuya and Pichilemu are an hour's drive away.
matanzas.rating_basis: A PWA/IWT Wave World Cup venue since 2023. The PWA rates the port-tack conditions here among the best in South America, and pros compare the wave to Ho'okipa. Boards and Windsurf UK note the reliable surazo and a cluster of wave spots nearby (Topocalma, Pupuya). Rating lowered for the cold water, the current and the limited tourist infrastructure
matanzas.waves_note: A powerful, fast left-hand wave spot for port-tack riding. The first section breaks in front of the rocks, then the bottom turns to sand and the wave gets faster and steeper. Long-period Pacific swell: usually 1–3 m, mast-high and bigger during PWA finals. The shape depends on the tide and the sandbank, which shifts from year to year
matanzas.hazards: Rocks at the first section and by the point, gusts near the cliff, a strong current that drags you into the impact zone. Heavy wipeouts on the shallow sandbank in big swell. Cold water. Sea lions (harmless, but can give you a fright)
matanzas.gustiness_note: The southerly surazo usually arrives by 11:00–13:00 and holds until evening (around 20:00), often in spells of 3–4 days. Lighter near the shore than further out, gusty near the rocks
matanzas.crowd_note: Many pros spend their winter here, so the local level on the wave is high, with its own priority rules (what counts is who's deeper on the wave, not who arrived first). Lots of surfers at weekends. There are quieter spots nearby
matanzas.region: Navidad, O'Higgins Region, central coast of Chile
matanzas.events: Chile World Cup, a PWA/IWT Wave World Cup event (since 2023): late March – early April in 2024 and 2025, 14–29 November in 2026
matanzas.launch: The sandy beach of Matanzas village by the Surazo hotel; getting in and out is easy. You need to be confident getting through the surf: in a swell you head out through the shorebreak and a strong current. On small days the wave suits those just starting out in waves. Beginners sail on flat water at the Rapel river mouth (La Boca), a 10-minute drive away
matanzas.sail_note: Most often 4.5–5.3 m² and 76–93 l boards: at the PWA event the pros used 4.2–5.3. 3.7–4.0 in a strong surazo
pros: World-class port-tack wave
Reliable side-shore wind from October to February
Plenty of wave spots within an hour
Flat water for learning at the nearby Rapel river mouth
cons: Cold water (12–15 °C) all year round, you need a 4/3–5/3 wetsuit
Strong current, heavy surf in a swell
Little rental of unknown quality: better bring your own
Many spots require a 4×4
matanzas.wind_dir: S–SSW (surazo), side-shore from the left, side-onshore in places
matanzas.airport: SCL — Santiago, ~2–2.5 hours by car (about 160 km via Route 78)
matanzas.rental_price_note: 25,000–30,000 pesos per day for a board, two sails, wetsuit and harness at the Olas de Matanzas campsite shop (Boards, 2012); gear is limited, better bring your own
school_notes: campsite with cabins and a small shop: limited windsurf gear rental, best booked in advance (2012 data)

lake-arenal.description: Lake Arenal is a large reservoir in the mountains of northern Costa Rica, at the foot of the Arenal volcano. From December to March the Caribbean trade wind accelerates between the ranges and blows 20–30 knots almost every day. On the north shore by the Tico Wind centre people sail 4–5 m² sails over the hard lake chop — classic bump & jump on warm fresh water.
lake-arenal.rating_basis: A legendary spot of the '80s and '90s: the wind here is said to be one of the strongest and most consistent in the northern hemisphere in winter. According to Tico Wind, it blows over 20 knots on about 75% of days in January and February; iWindsurf forum users praise the chop for bump & jump. Rating lowered because only one centre is left (it was temporarily closed in 2021), for the gusts near the shore and the short season
lake-arenal.waves_note: A freshwater reservoir about 30 km long: over a 10 km fetch the wind kicks up hard lake chop and wind swell over a metre high, great ramps for jumping. One tack is noticeably bumpier than the other
lake-arenal.hazards: The wind is slightly offshore: if you break gear or get tired, you drift to the middle of the lake and towards the volcano, and you may not make it back upwind (the centre keeps a rescue jet ski). Strong, gusty wind and waves over a metre high — steep for a lake; beginners find it hard to keep getting up after falling
lake-arenal.gustiness_note: The Caribbean trade wind accelerates between the mountains, with a steady direction (NE–ENE). The wind is slightly offshore, so it's gusty right by the shore. With passing cold fronts it can blow 30 knots for 4–5 days in a row. In winter it blows day and night
lake-arenal.crowd_note: Not many windsurfers: the spot's heyday was in the '80s and '90s, and now there are more kiters and wing foilers. Plenty of room on the water
lake-arenal.launch: A small area on the north shore by the Tico Wind centre: gear is rigged on the grass and you launch from a little beach. The centre is on Route 142, about 14 km from Tilarán towards Nuevo Arenal, with a dirt track down to the shore (no 4×4 needed). With your own gear you pay a water access fee. A rescue jet ski is on standby on the water
lake-arenal.sail_note: Most people use 4.0–5.0 m² and 76–95 l boards. 3.5 and smaller on strong days, 5.5–6.0 at the start and end of the season
pros: Strong, reliable wind almost every day from December to March
Warm fresh water, a shorty is enough
Ramps on the chop, plenty of room on the water
Volcano, hot springs and rainforest nearby
cons: Effectively just one centre; it was temporarily closed in 2021 — check its status before you go
Expensive rental (about $109 a day in 2019–2020)
Slightly offshore wind, gusty near the shore
The wind is usually too strong for beginners
Rainy season and light wind from May to October
lake-arenal.wind_dir: NE–ENE trade wind, side-shore / side-off from the left
lake-arenal.airport: LIR — Liberia, ~1.5–2 hours by car; SJO — San José, ~3.5 hours
lake-arenal.rental_price_note: per day of rental at Tico Wind, with lunch on the beach; a week costs $584–641. Newer price lists say “on request”
school_notes: centre running since 1991: Fanatic boards, Duotone sails, a gear pool (you can swap boards and sails), windsurf, kite and foil lessons, rescue jet ski. Main season December–April; the rest of the year they open when there's wind

sal-santa-maria.description: Sal is Cape Verde's main windsurf destination: from November to May a steady north-easterly trade wind blows, and winter Atlantic swells bring waves. The base is Santa Maria bay with several centres (side-off from the left, freeride and foil); nearby are the easy wave at Ponta Leme and the legendary Ponta Preta, which has hosted PWA World Cup events.
sal-santa-maria.rating_basis: Surf Magazin, Windsurf Magazine and Waterwind: a steady winter trade wind and Ponta Preta — Cape Verde's “star wave” and a PWA venue; Santa Maria bay is good for freeride and foil. Downside — conditions are a bit tough for beginners (side-off, shorebreak)
sal-santa-maria.waves_note: In Santa Maria bay — chop and a small shorebreak, flat water beyond the pier, and further out swell for beginners in waves; Ponta Leme is the island's easiest wave, with flat water inside; Ponta Preta (5–10 minutes west) is a powerful, steep world-class wave by the rocks, 2–4 m+ in winter swells
sal-santa-maria.hazards: Side-offshore wind in the bay (don't sail alone — if you break gear, help is far away); shorebreak and rocks at Ponta Preta, frequent gear breakages; reefs and a strong current at Ponta Sino; sea urchins at the northern spots; sharks are sometimes seen on the east coast — stay out of the water at dusk
sal-santa-maria.gustiness_note: The trade wind is steady, usually 14–20 knots, 25–30 from mid-January to March–April; in the bay the wind is side-off — there can be holes and gusts near the shore and behind buildings; at Ponta Leme the wind is steadier
sal-santa-maria.crowd_note: Ponta Preta and Ponta Leme get crowded in a good swell (surfers, kiters; surfers have priority at Ponta Preta); the bay and Kite Beach are spacious
sal-santa-maria.region: Sal, south of the island (Santa Maria bay)
sal-santa-maria.events: PWA Wave World Cup events at Ponta Preta (2007–2010; in 2010 the season final in November); in 2025 a Wingfoil World Cup event (waves)
sal-santa-maria.launch: Sandy beach in the eastern part of Santa Maria bay by the centres (ION Club Ponta Leme, Club Angulo): a light shorebreak, and staff help you through it with your gear. From here you can sail upwind to Ponta Leme or downwind to Ponta Sino. At Ponta Preta you launch through the shorebreak, sometimes waiting up to 20 minutes for a lull, with rocks nearby
sal-santa-maria.sail_note: Usually 4.5–5.3 m², 3.7–4.5 m² in January–April at 25–30 knots; on the Ponta Preta wave most often 4.0–4.7
pros: Steady trade wind from November to May
Warm water and sunshine in winter
World-class Ponta Preta wave within walking distance
Direct charters from Europe, several centres
cons: Side-off wind in the bay — if you break gear, you can be blown away from shore
Shorebreak and rocks at the wave spots, not for beginners
Almost no wind in summer (August–September)
Very crowded at Ponta Preta on good days
sal-santa-maria.wind_dir: NE–ENE (trade wind), side-offshore / side-shore from the left
school_notes: Two centres in Santa Maria; Fanatic / Duotone windsurf rental at Ponta Leme, help through the shorebreak, storage; 9:00–17:00
Josh Angulo's centre — the classic launch point in the bay, with a bar and café next door
Club hotel 5 minutes from Ponta Preta, gear included with your stay (certificate required)

fehmarn-wulfener-hals.description: Wulfener Hals is a spit in the south of Fehmarn island between the open Baltic and the shallow Burger Binnensee lagoon, and one of Germany's most popular windsurf spots. You can stand almost everywhere in the lagoon and the water is flat — ideal for learning, freeriding and freestyle, while regattas are held on the sea side. It works best in an easterly, especially in spring, but the spot handles almost any direction, and the island has a dozen more spots.
fehmarn-wulfener-hals.rating_basis: Fehmarn is Germany's most popular windsurf island, with a dozen spots for every wind direction; Surf Magazin calls Wulfener Hals “a paradise for all levels” with a huge shallow area; Windfinder lists it among Germany's most popular spots. Downsides — cool water and seaweed
fehmarn-wulfener-hals.waves_note: Flat water on the Burger Binnensee lagoon, with short chop in strong wind; on the open Baltic (through the campsite) — chop and small wind waves, where regattas are held
fehmarn-wulfener-hals.hazards: Long fins hit the bottom in the shallows; the small stretch of water by the marina is awkward to sail; chop on the sea side in strong wind; cold water outside summer
fehmarn-wulfener-hals.gustiness_note: Low shoreline and open space — the wind is generally steady; slightly gustier near the shore in westerlies
fehmarn-wulfener-hals.crowd_note: Lots of people on the water and in the car parks in summer and at weekends; quieter in spring and autumn, and on the island you can always move to another spot
fehmarn-wulfener-hals.events: Surf-Festival Fehmarn — a big windsurf test festival with the Racer of the Sea regatta and the German Freestyle Challenge, on Fehmarn's neighbouring South Beach (Südstrand); in 2026 on 14–17 May (possibly the last time at this venue)
fehmarn-wulfener-hals.launch: Sandy shore and a “surf meadow” for rigging on the southern shore of the Burger Binnensee lagoon by the Wulfener Hals campsite (Wulfener-Hals-Weg); day parking in front of the campsite gates and on the meadow opposite the golf course (paid in season). You can stand almost everywhere; to reach the open Baltic, go through the campsite or carry your gear a few metres across the spit
fehmarn-wulfener-hals.sail_note: Usually 5.5–7.0 m² on a freeride board, 4.5–5.3 in strong wind; 3.5–5.0 for beginners in the shallows
pros: Huge flat-water shallows — ideal for beginners and practising tricks
Works in almost any wind direction
Big centre, campsite and car parks right by the water
An island with a dozen spots for different winds
cons: Cool water: up to 18–19 °C in summer, and you need a warm wetsuit in spring and autumn
Seaweed from May to November
Crowded in summer, paid parking
Shallow — long fins catch the bottom
fehmarn-wulfener-hals.wind_dir: E–SE and NE (a thermally boosted easterly in spring) are best; NW–N also work, with long runs towards Burg (Burg auf Fehmarn); SW–W are the most frequent
fehmarn-wulfener-hals.airport: HAM — Hamburg, ~1 h 45 min (~150 km); CPH — Copenhagen, ~2.5–3 h with the Rødby – Puttgarden ferry
school_notes: VDWS centre at the Wulfener Hals campsite (part of Windsurfing Hamburg): courses, rental, surf camps, shop; open April to October
school on South Beach opposite, across the lagoon

sylt-westerland.description: Westerland on Sylt is Germany's main wave spot and the stage for the most famous PWA World Cup event, which draws around 200,000 spectators every autumn. The North Sea delivers strong, steady low-pressure winds, a sandbar with waves and a hard shorebreak at high tide; side-shore winds from the southwest and north work best. This is a spot for experienced sailors: longshore currents, stone groynes and cold water.
sylt-westerland.rating_basis: Germany's main wave spot and the venue of the most famous PWA World Cup event; Surf Magazin and local guides cite a powerful shorebreak, currents and groynes — “one of Germany's toughest spots”. For strong riders; the cold water and fickle shorebreak lower the rating
sylt-westerland.waves_note: A beach break with a sandbar: at low tide the wave breaks on the bar, at high tide the sets reach the beach and the shorebreak gets hard; in storms during the World Cup the waves are 3–4 m, 1–2 m on ordinary windy days. Often flat in summer when there's no wind
sylt-westerland.hazards: Strong currents along the shore and between the groynes; remains of stone groynes reach ~20 m out to sea every 100–200 m (poorly visible at high tide outside the season, marked with yellow crosses); a powerful shorebreak that snaps masts; a tidal range of ~2–3 m
sylt-westerland.gustiness_note: The wind from Atlantic lows is steady and strong; right by the shore it's lighter than further out, so you need some extra power; squalls on stormy days
sylt-westerland.crowd_note: On ordinary days there aren't many people on the water — the spot weeds out beginners; on good wave days and during the World Cup the beach is packed
sylt-westerland.events: Citroën Windsurf World Cup Sylt — the biggest annual PWA event (Grand Slam), on Brandenburger Strand; in 2026 on 25 September – 4 October: waves (men and women), freestyle, foil slalom; around 200,000 spectators
sylt-westerland.launch: Launch straight from the beach by the promenade in southern Westerland (at the end of Brandenburger Straße), next to the Sunset Beach / Duotone Pro Center. Parking behind the dune on Brandenburger Straße (from free to ~€18 a day depending on the season); until 18:00 the guest card (Kurkarte) is checked at the beach entrance. Getting out through the shorebreak in an onshore wind is very hard
sylt-westerland.sail_note: The spot works from 20 kn: usually 4.2–5.3 m², 3.7–4.2 in autumn storms; foil or 6–7 m² in light summer wind
pros: Real North Sea waves and strong wind
Legendary PWA World Cup event every autumn
Launch straight from the town beach, with a centre and cafés nearby
Airport on the island
cons: Cold water even in summer (up to 17–18 °C), you need a wetsuit
Hard shorebreak at high tide, tough to get out in onshore wind
Currents and remains of stone groynes
Resort tax and paid parking
sylt-westerland.wind_dir: SW and N–NNE — side-shore (best); W–NW — onshore, tough to get out
sylt-westerland.airport: GWT — Sylt (Westerland), ~10 minutes; HAM — Hamburg, ~3–3.5 h (train or car train across the Hindenburgdamm)
school_notes: right on Brandenburger Strand: windsurfing, kite, surfing, SUP, rental; open 1 April to 31 October
in neighbouring Wenningstedt (~3 km north): surf centre with windsurfing

cabarete.description: Cabarete is the windsurf capital of the Caribbean, on the north coast of the Dominican Republic. In a wide, reef-protected bay a thermally boosted trade wind blows during the day: the inner bay is great for learning and bump & jump, while the reef 800 m offshore has waves. The best wind is from June to August; the best combination of wind and waves is from February to April.
cabarete.rating_basis: A Caribbean windsurfing classic since the 1980s: steady trade wind, a bay for all levels and reef waves. Covered in detail by Boards and Surf Magazin. Downsides — crowds of kiters and wing foilers, hectic traffic
cabarete.waves_note: Chop inside the bay. On the reef about 800 m from shore the waves are usually shoulder- to head-high; 2–5 m in a northerly swell from February to April. An ocean wave, fairly gentle, breaking at an angle to the wind
cabarete.hazards: Shallow by the reef (watch your fins); the reef in a big swell is no place for beginners or the unsure; sea urchins at Encuentro; kiters downwind; wind shadow at the upwind end of the bay. Don't walk on deserted beaches in the evening
cabarete.gustiness_note: The trade wind is boosted by the thermal: light in the morning, Force 5–6 by lunchtime. Windguru forecasts often underestimate the wind. In December–January the wind is stronger but gustier
cabarete.crowd_note: The bay is shared by windsurfers, kiters, wing foilers and SUPers. Kiters mostly keep to the downwind part (Bozo Beach and Kite Beach)
cabarete.launch: Sandy beach in the centre of town, with the centres right by the water. Usually only a small shorebreak. The best place to launch is the middle of the bay: at the upwind end there's wind shadow near the shore, and the downwind part (Bozo Beach) is already the kite zone
cabarete.sail_note: Usually 4.7–5.7 m², 4.2–4.7 on strong days; 6.0–7.0 in the mornings and on light days
pros: Steady, thermally boosted trade wind, 250–300 windy days a year
A bay for all levels, with reef waves nearby
Warm water, 26–29 °C all year round
Lots of centres, restaurants and accommodation right on the beach
Other spots nearby: flat-water La Boca and the Encuentro waves
cons: Crowded: kiters, wings and SUPs in the same bay
No wind in the morning, sailing is mostly in the afternoon
Chaotic traffic and petty theft
cabarete.wind_dir: E–ENE trade wind, cross-shore from right to left (starboard tack), side-on in places
school_notes: the biggest centre, in the middle of the bay between two reefs: JP and Starboard boards, NeilPryde sails, windsurf and windfoil lessons
Bozo Beach, Villa Taina hotel, about 200 m downwind of Vela; rental, lessons for all levels

dahab-lagoon-windsurf.description: Dahab in Sinai is one of the Red Sea's main windsurf resorts. A northerly wind off the mountains blows almost all year round, most often at 15–25 knots, and everything is in one place: a shallow lagoon for beginners, the smooth Speedy speed strip behind the sand spit and waves beyond Napoleon reef. There are several big centres, including Russian-speaking ones.
dahab-lagoon-windsurf.rating_basis: One of the best-known windsurf resorts on the Red Sea (Boards, Windsurf UK): wind almost all year round (~20 knots on a typical day, ≥4 Bft on 77–87% of days in summer), three zones close together — a lagoon for beginners, the smooth Speedy speed strip and waves beyond the reef; gusts near the shore and summer heat
dahab-lagoon-windsurf.waves_note: Flat water and light chop in the lagoon and at Speedy behind the sand spit; waves (swell up to 2–3 m on windy days) only outside, beyond Napoleon reef (the “Kamikaze” zone), for advanced sailors
dahab-lagoon-windsurf.hazards: Offshore wind (without boat cover you get blown out), corals and reefs along the edges of the lagoon and outside, strong wind and swell in the “Kamikaze” zone beyond the reef, students in the lagoon, sun and heat
dahab-lagoon-windsurf.gustiness_note: The wind blows off the mountains, so near the shore by the centres there's wind shadow and gusts; at Speedy and on the far side of the spit the wind is stronger and steadier
dahab-lagoon-windsurf.crowd_note: Lots of students in the inner lagoon, dozens of riders at Speedy on a typical day; kiters ride in a separate kite lagoon
dahab-lagoon-windsurf.region: South Sinai, Gulf of Aqaba (Red Sea)
dahab-lagoon-windsurf.launch: A gently sloping sandy beach on the inner side of the lagoon (Lagoon Club, Swiss Inn, Safir and other hotels), no shorebreak; the inner part of the lagoon is standing depth — handy for learning. To Speedy (the smooth speed strip behind the sand spit) and Baby Bay the centres take you by boat, or you walk along the spit
dahab-lagoon-windsurf.sail_note: Usually 4.7–5.8 m² (a typical day is ~20 knots); 4.0–4.5 on strong summer days at Speedy, 6.5–7.5 on light winter days. The centres have sails up to 8.5 m²
pros: Wind almost all year round, planing almost every day in summer
Horseshoe lagoon: you drift onto the spit, safe for learning
Smooth Speedy for speed and freestyle, waves outside for advanced sailors
Warm water all year round, Russian-speaking instructors available
cons: Offshore wind: gusty and wind shadow by the centres
Summer heat up to 38 °C
In winter the wind is lighter and it's cool on the water (3/2 wetsuit)
dahab-lagoon-windsurf.wind_dir: N–NNE, offshore / side-offshore from the left; the horseshoe lagoon means you drift onto the spit rather than out to the open sea
dahab-lagoon-windsurf.airport: SSH — Sharm El Sheikh, ~1 h (about 85–90 km)
school_notes: on the grounds of the Swiss Inn Resort in the lagoon; courses in Russian, English and Arabic; RRD sails, slalom and foil available
windsurfing and kite in the lagoon; according to tonkosti.ru, most instructors speak Russian
two centres (Lagoon Club & Resort and Jaz Dahabeya), 300+ JP / NeilPryde boards and sails, all year round, boat rescue
at the Safir Dahab Resort, Fanatic boards and Duotone sails, boat shuttle to Speedy

soma-bay-safaga.description: Soma Bay is a sheltered bay on the Ras Abu Soma peninsula north of Safaga, and one of the windiest places on Egypt's Red Sea coast.
